newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Identity crisis looms as HK finds real parents.
newsitem.headline: Identity crisis looms as HK finds real parents.

text.p: When Hong Kong, like an adopted child, returns to its true parents on the Chinese mainland, there will be stiff psychological knots to untie, psychiatrists said.
"Identity crisis is a problem quite ambivalent in Hong Kong," Professor of Psychiatry Felice Lieh-Mak of the University of Hong Kong told Reuters.
"People are proud to be Chinese but they are also ashamed because of the way the international community has pictured China and demonised it," Lieh-Mak said.
In less than a week, Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule after more than 150 years as a British colony.
"The transition has reminded many Hong Kong people that they belong to the Chinese race," clinical psychiatrist Pang Wing Luk said.

Mandarin, the official dialect of mainland China, is becoming fashionable in traditionally Cantonese-speaking Hong Kong, with Mandarin classes, pop records and radio stations taking a slice of the markets.

"In any change of sovereignty, there is a tendency to throw out everything that belonged to the previous colonial government -- the language, the culture, the value -- this is not very rational," Lieh-Mak, who is also president of the World Psychiatric Association, said.
Hong Kong citizens, who were kept politically silent for most of the years of British autocratic rule, have lately awakened to nationalist pride.

Hong Kong activists last year joined protesters in China after an ultra-rightwing Japanese group erected a makeshift lighthouse on one of the disputed Diaoyu (Senkaku) islands. One Hong Kong activist drowned after leaping into the stormy sea in defiance of a Japanese blockade.

Poignant feelings of national solidarity and shame took one million people on to the streets of the territory for the first time in June 1989, after Chinese army tanks crushed pro-democracy protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Other contradictions also dampen the handover excitement.
"For instance, having a foreign passport gives you a lot more respect, and that really pours cold water on the sense of pride of being Chinese," Lieh-Mak said.
A large proportion of Hong Kong residents have obtained passports from Europe, Australia, the United States or Canada, many spurred by the Tiananmen carnage.
"China has been a threatening, carrot-and-stick parent that says 'you do your job, you bring in the money, you make everyone happy'," Lieh-Mak said.
"Hong Kong will miss its adopted father and take a while to forge a relationship with the new one," Pang said.
Psychiatrists and social workers however said Hong Kong people, known for their keen, business-oriented pragmatism, are likely to take the transition in their stride.
"When so much is unknown, there will be a tendency to be more superstitious and religious," Lieh-Mak said. "But Hong Kong people are very practical."
A director at the Samaritans in Hong Kong, who counsel people tempted by suicide, said she had heard of almost no distress case related to the handover.
